title: Dieter Rams: As Little Design as Possible
author: Sophie Lovell
description:
The most complete monograph on Dieter Rams, the German industrial designer behind decades of Braun products and Vitsœ furniture. Sophie Lovell follows his career through objects, sketches and archive photographs.

The book also sets out the ten principles of good design he is best known for, and shows how they were applied to radios, record players, shavers and shelving.
summary: The definitive monograph on Dieter Rams, the designer behind Braun and Vitsœ and the ten principles of good design.
editorNote: If you only buy one monograph, this is the one. It makes a convincing case that restraint is a method, not a style.

title: Charles & Ray Eames: Designers of the Twentieth Century
author: Pat Kirkham
description:
A scholarly and richly illustrated account of the Eames Office, from the moulded plywood chair to films, exhibitions and architecture. Kirkham places the couple’s work in the context of postwar American culture.

She also looks closely at how the office actually operated, including Ray’s often understated contribution to its output.
summary: A scholarly, richly illustrated account of the Eames Office, from moulded plywood chairs to films and exhibitions.
editorNote: Read it for the process: prototypes, failures and iteration are documented as carefully as the finished icons.

title: Jasper Morrison: Everything but the Walls
author: Jasper Morrison
description:
A survey of Jasper Morrison’s work in his own words, covering furniture, tableware, lighting and appliances from the 1980s onwards.

It is a good introduction to an attitude associated with his work: restraint, usability and the belief that an object should earn its place in a room.
summary: A survey of Jasper Morrison’s furniture, tableware and appliances, in his own words.
editorNote: A calm book about calm objects. Useful if your own sketches tend to have one feature too many.

title: Achille Castiglioni: Complete Works
author: Sergio Polano
description:
The reference monograph on the Milanese designer behind the Arco and Toio lamps, the Mezzadro stool and dozens of everyday objects. It catalogues the work project by project.

The book shows how Castiglioni’s humour and his habit of reusing found components shaped Italian industrial design.
summary: The reference monograph on the Milanese designer behind the Arco lamp and Mezzadro stool.
editorNote: Essential for anyone interested in how wit and industrial production can live in the same object.

title: Autoprogettazione?
author: Enzo Mari
description:
Enzo Mari’s project for self-built furniture: a set of simple plans anyone can follow with rough timber, nails and a saw.

Both a practical manual and a statement about design, production and who gets to make things.
summary: Enzo Mari’s plans for self-built furniture: simple designs anyone can make with rough timber, nails and a saw.
editorNote: Build one of the tables and you will understand his argument about proportion and effort better than any essay could.

title: Materials and Design: The Art and Science of Material Selection in Product Design
author: Michael F. Ashby & Kara Johnson
description:
A rigorous but designer-friendly guide to how materials are chosen for products. Ashby and Johnson pair engineering property charts with the softer qualities (texture, warmth, sound) that shape how an object feels.

The book shows how to reconcile the two in real briefs.
summary: A rigorous, designer-friendly guide to choosing materials, pairing engineering data with how materials feel.
editorNote: The property charts alone are worth it. Keep it next to your sketchbook when you are deciding between two plausible materials.

title: Making It: Manufacturing Techniques for Product Design
author: Chris Lefteri
description:
A visual guide to the manufacturing processes behind everyday products, from injection moulding and die casting to sheet-metal forming and woodworking.

Each process gets a clear explanation, typical applications and examples, so designers know what is possible before they draw it.
summary: A visual guide to the manufacturing processes behind everyday products, with applications and examples.
editorNote: The one to hand to a student who asks how anything is actually made.

title: Materials for Design
author: Victoria Ballard Bell & Patrick Rand
description:
A compact catalogue of materials used by designers and architects, organised by family with notes on properties and applications.

Handy as a first reference when a project reaches the stage of choosing between wood, metal, plastic or glass.
summary: A compact catalogue of materials used by designers and architects, with notes on properties and uses.
editorNote: Small, visual and quick to consult. A good companion to the heavier engineering references.

title: Design for the Real World: Human Ecology and Social Change
author: Victor Papanek
description:
A landmark, deliberately provocative argument that designers have a social and ecological responsibility. Papanek criticises wasteful, status-driven products and makes the case for designing for real needs.

Dated in places, it remains widely taught and widely argued with.
summary: Papanek’s landmark argument that designers have a social and ecological responsibility.
editorNote: Read it as an argument rather than a manual. The provocations still work.

title: The Language of Things
author: Deyan Sudjic
description:
An essay on how objects communicate status, taste and identity, from luxury goods to mass-produced gadgets.

Sudjic, a former director of the Design Museum, writes clearly about why we want the things we want.
summary: An essay on how objects communicate status, taste and identity, by a former Design Museum director.
editorNote: Short, sharp and easy to read in a weekend.

title: Pioneers of Modern Design: From William Morris to Walter Gropius
author: Nikolaus Pevsner
description:
The classic history of how the Arts and Crafts movement and the early industrial age led to modern design, from William Morris to Walter Gropius.

Its thesis is contested now, but it remains the starting point for understanding the story modernism told about itself.
summary: The classic history of how the Arts and Crafts movement led to modern design, from Morris to Gropius.
editorNote: Read it critically. Much of the current debate about modernism starts as a reaction to this book.

title: Cradle to Cradle: Remaking the Way We Make Things
author: Michael Braungart & William McDonough
description:
A manifesto for designing products as part of continuous material cycles rather than one-way trips to landfill.

Influential in sustainable product design, it introduces the idea of technical and biological nutrients.
summary: A manifesto for designing products as part of continuous material cycles rather than one-way trips to landfill.
editorNote: Its ideas now sit behind much of the circular-design conversation.

title: The Design of Everyday Things
author: Don Norman
description:
The standard text on usability and human-centred design. Norman explains affordances, signifiers, feedback and mental models through doors, stoves and light switches.

He shows why blaming users for errors is usually a design failure.
summary: The standard text on usability and human-centred design, told through doors, stoves and light switches.
editorNote: Every designer should read this once. You will notice badly designed doors for the rest of your life.

title: Product Design and Development
author: Karl T. Ulrich & Steven D. Eppinger
description:
A textbook that follows a product from opportunity identification to launch, covering concept generation, industrial design, prototyping and economics.

Closer to the business of product development than to the craft of form, and useful for that reason.
summary: A textbook following a product from opportunity to launch: concepts, industrial design, prototyping and economics.
editorNote: Not glamorous, but it explains how a team actually gets a product out of the door.

title: Sketching: Drawing Techniques for Product Designers
author: Koos Eissen & Roselien Steur
description:
A practical course in perspective, shading and rendering aimed at product and industrial designers, with worked examples from professionals.

Good to practise from, pencil in hand.
summary: A practical course in perspective, shading and rendering for product and industrial designers.
editorNote: Work through the first chapters and your sketches will improve within a few weeks.

title: Industrial Design A–Z
author: Charlotte & Peter Fiell
description:
An alphabetical reference to the designers and companies that shaped industrial design in the twentieth century, illustrated throughout.

A browsing book as much as a reference one.
summary: An alphabetical reference to the designers and companies that shaped twentieth-century industrial design.
editorNote: Excellent for discovering names you will want to look up properly afterwards.

title: Furniture Design: An Introduction to Development, Materials and Manufacturing
author: Stuart Lawson
description:
A practical introduction to how furniture gets designed and made, covering concept development, materials, joinery and industrial production methods.

Case studies from contemporary makers and manufacturers show the ideas in practice.
summary: A practical introduction to how furniture is designed and made, with case studies from contemporary makers.
editorNote: The best single starting point for furniture design.

title: Understanding Wood: A Craftsman’s Guide to Wood Technology
author: R. Bruce Hoadley
description:
A clear technical guide to wood as a material: how it grows, moves with humidity, and behaves when cut and joined.

Essential for anyone designing in timber who wants their pieces to survive the first winter.
summary: A clear technical guide to wood as a material: growth, movement with humidity, and behaviour when cut and joined.
editorNote: Explains why drawers stick and tabletops split, which is most of furniture design in one sentence.

title: The Chair: Rethinking Culture, Body, and Design
author: Galen Cranz
description:
A history and critique of the chair as a designed object, asking why people sit the way they do and how chair design relates to the body.

Useful background for anyone designing seating.
summary: A history and critique of the chair as a designed object, and of why we sit the way we do.
editorNote: Makes you question whether the chair is the right answer at all.

title: Thinking with Type
author: Ellen Lupton
description:
A compact guide to typography for designers, organised into letter, text and grid with clear do’s and don’ts.

Short, visual and practical.
summary: A compact, practical guide to typography organised into letter, text and grid.
editorNote: Short enough to read in an evening and useful for years.

title: Grid Systems in Graphic Design
author: Josef Müller-Brockmann
description:
The definitive manual on designing with grids, from a leading figure of Swiss graphic design.

Diagrams, examples and a strict rationale for structure.
summary: The definitive manual on designing with grids, from a leading figure of Swiss graphic design.
editorNote: The source of many of the layouts you admire.

title: Designing Design
author: Kenya Hara
description:
Kenya Hara, art director of Muji, reflects on design as a way of seeing the everyday, including the idea of emptiness.

A quiet, image-led book.
summary: Kenya Hara, art director of Muji, on design as a way of seeing the everyday and the idea of emptiness.
editorNote: Read it slowly. It is more about attention than technique.
